title: Private ERM and private online learning

items.title: Randomized weighted majority with full information

references.title: Cynthia Dwork and Aaron Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy, Chapter 11 §11.2

items.statement_or_definition: For k,T≥1, η>0, and loss vectors ℓ_t∈[0,1]^k, initialize w_{1,j}=1. At each round draw a_t=j with probability w_{t,j}/∑_r w_{t,r}, observe the full vector ℓ_t, and update w_{t+1,j}=w_{t,j}exp(−ηℓ_t(j)). Return the action transcript.
proof_obligations: Show finite positive normalizers and measurability of the finite action probability kernels.
items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used to define the finite-round procedure.

items.title: Finite-class empirical-risk selection with exponential weights

references.title: Cynthia Dwork and Aaron Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy, Chapter 3 §3.4 and Chapter 11 §11.1
Salil Vadhan, The Complexity of Differential Privacy, 2017 manuscript, §4.2

items.statement_or_definition: For n≥1, ε>0, a nonempty finite class C of measurable binary classifiers, and a finite labeled sample or multiset D of size m≥n, define L̂_D(h)=m⁻¹∑_{(x,y)∈D}1{h(x)≠y}. Output h∈C with probability proportional to exp(−εnL̂_D(h)/2), using 1/n as a sensitivity upper-bound scale.
proof_obligations: Verify the mismatch losses and sample-dependent probabilities are measurable, all weights are finite and positive, and the normalization defines a probability kernel.
items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used for finite normalization or measurability.

items.title: Private online learning regret under composition
items.axiom_use: The expected potential bound and per-round likelihood-ratio proof use no choice principle. AC is assumed for the Azuma–Hoeffding high-probability regret bound and for arbitrary-measurable-output advanced composition.

references.title: Cynthia Dwork and Aaron Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy, Chapter 11 §11.2
Salil Vadhan, The Complexity of Differential Privacy, 2017 manuscript, §2.2

items.statement_or_definition: For k,T≥1 and full-information losses ℓ_t∈[0,1]^k fixed before each fresh action draw but allowed to depend on the previous transcript, define average regret R_T=T⁻¹∑_tℓ_t(a_t)−min_jT⁻¹∑_tℓ_t(j). For every η>0, E R_T≤η+ln(k)/(ηT); under AC, with probability at least 1−β, R_T≤η+ln(k)/(ηT)+√(ln(1/β)/(2T)). For k=1 regret is zero; for k≥2, η=√(ln(k)/T) gives expected bound 2√(ln(k)/T). For fixed loss sequences adjacent by arbitrary replacement of one full time-step vector, each prior-history action kernel is (2η,0)-DP. Under AC and ε>0, 0<δ<1, L=ln(1/δ), choosing η=min{ε/√(32TL),1/2,√(ε/(16T))} makes the full transcript (ε,δ)-DP. With this η the exact high-probability regret cap is η+(ln(k)/T)max{√(32TL)/ε,2,4√(T/ε)}+√(ln(1/β)/(2T)); η₀=ε/√(32TL) is retained when ε≤√(8TL) and ε≤2L, giving η₀+√(32L)ln(k)/(ε√T)+√(ln(1/β)/(2T)). The same privacy conclusion holds for interactive adjacent strategies when every common-history next-action kernel satisfies the ordered (2η,0) event inequalities.
proof_obligations: Prove the finite log-partition potential bound for η≤1, handle η>1 directly, and derive expected and high-probability regret for nonanticipating adaptive losses using the predictable-interval martingale tail.

Prove each prior-history action-kernel event inequality under whole-vector replacement and check all three advanced-composition caps, the exact inverse-η regret expression, the source-choice region, and the interactive-kernel extension.

items.title: Private finite-class ERM excess-risk bound
items.axiom_use: No form of the Axiom of Choice is used in the local privacy, utility, and sample-complexity arguments. The finite-class deviation supplier states its argument is choice-free; this item remains escalated until the supplier readiness record is reconciled.

references.title: Cynthia Dwork and Aaron Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy, Chapter 3 §3.4 and Chapter 11 §11.1
Shai Shalev-Shwartz and Shai Ben-David, Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms, Chapter 4 §4.2

items.statement_or_definition: For a nonempty measurable instance space X, for finite labeled databases of size at least n, with add/remove neighbors required to remain in the domain, the empirical zero-one risk has sensitivity at most 1/n and the finite-class selector with weights exp(−εn L̂_D(h)/2) is pure ε-DP. For n IID examples from any distribution and a finite nonempty measurable binary class C, with probability at least 1−β the selector has population excess risk at most 2√((ln|C|+ln(4/β))/(2n))+(2/(εn))(ln|C|+ln(2/β)). For |C|≥2, n≥24 max{(ln|C|+ln(1/β))/(εα),(ln|C|+ln(1/β))/α²} suffices for excess at most α; for |C|=1, the excess is zero. The privacy proof uses 1/n as an upper-bound scale, and the statistical bound is choice-free.
proof_obligations: Prove the pairwise add/remove sensitivity bound on the size-restricted domain, the normalized-weight ordered DP ratios, and the finite-range selector utility tail using the conservative 1/n scale.

Combine the utility event with the choice-free two-sided finite-class deviation event, derive the stated constants by a union bound, and handle the singleton class and all 0<alpha,beta<1 boundary regimes.

title: Private ERM and private online learning — Examples

items.title: Replacing one full loss vector changes a later action kernel

references.title: Cynthia Dwork and Aaron Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy, Chapter 11 §11.2

items.statement_or_definition: For k=2 and T=3, compare the all-zero loss sequence with the sequence whose second loss vector is (1,0) and whose other vectors are zero. These inputs differ by replacement of one full time-step vector; the first two action kernels agree and the third has weights (e^(−η),1) instead of (1,1).
proof_obligations: Verify the whole-vector adjacency and compute the two third-round distributions from the online algorithm.
items.axiom_use: The finite calculation uses no choice axiom; any transcript privacy conclusion is the theorem's AC-dependent result.
items.statement: Let $k=2$, $T=3$, and $\eta>0$. Compare the all-zero loss sequence with the sequence whose second loss vector is $(1,0)$ and whose first and third vectors are zero. These two fixed inputs differ by replacement of one complete time-step vector. For both inputs the first- and second-round action kernels are uniform on $\{1,2\}$. At round three the all-zero input has weights $(1,1)$ and probabilities $(1/2,1/2)$, while the replaced input has weights $(e^{-\eta},1)$ and probabilities $(1/(1+e^\eta),e^\eta/(1+e^\eta))$. In particular, the event that the third action is $1$ has probability ratio $(1+e^\eta)/2$ between the all-zero and replaced inputs.

items.title: Private ERM on a four-threshold class

references.title: Cynthia Dwork and Aaron Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy, Chapter 11 §11.1
Shai Shalev-Shwartz and Shai Ben-David, Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms, Chapter 4 §4.2

items.statement_or_definition: On X={0,1,2}, let h_r(x)=1{x≥r} for r∈{0,1,2,3}, and take D={(0,0),(1,1),(2,0)} with n=3. The empirical risks in order r=0,1,2,3 are 2/3,1/3,2/3,1/3, so the private selector assigns weights e^(−ε),e^(−ε/2),e^(−ε),e^(−ε/2).
proof_obligations: Compute each threshold's predictions and empirical risk, then normalize the four private-selection weights.

items.title: A finite class can make private ERM impractical

references.title: Cynthia Dwork and Aaron Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy, Chapter 11 §11.1
Shai Shalev-Shwartz and Shai Ben-David, Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms, Chapter 4 §4.2

items.statement_or_definition: For X={0,1}^d, let C contain every binary function on X, so |C|=2^(2^d). A direct implementation of the finite-class private selector evaluates each classifier on each of n sample points and normalizes one weight per classifier, requiring order n·2^(2^d) score evaluations; this is a cost of the direct enumeration, not a lower bound for every possible algorithm.
proof_obligations: Count the functions from a 2^d-point set to {0,1} and count the empirical-score evaluations in the specified direct implementation.
